work: For <sup>35</sup>Cl the mass number is 35 and Z = 17, so neutrons = A - Z = 35 - 17 = 18. Gaining an electron changes only the electron count, not the nucleus.
cleanExplanation: Chlorine has Z = 17, and the isotope is chlorine-35 (A = 35). Neutrons = A - Z = 35 - 17 = 18. The negative charge means one extra electron, which does not change the number of neutrons.

work: Na, Mg, Al and Cl are in the same period (period 3). Across a period, effective nuclear charge increases and radius decreases, so radius order is Na > Mg > Al > Cl.
cleanExplanation: These four elements are all in period 3. Moving left to right, added protons pull the same-shell electrons in more tightly, so atomic radius decreases: Na > Mg > Al > Cl. Sodium therefore has the largest radius.

work: CO<sub>2</sub> (linear), BF<sub>3</sub> (trigonal planar) and CH<sub>4</sub> (tetrahedral) have symmetric bond dipoles that cancel. NH<sub>3</sub> is trigonal pyramidal with a lone pair, so its dipoles do not cancel.
cleanExplanation: A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel. CO<sub>2</sub>, BF<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub> are symmetric, so their dipoles cancel. NH<sub>3</sub> is trigonal pyramidal with a lone pair on nitrogen, so the N-H dipoles add up to a net dipole.

work: Boyle's law at constant T: P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. P<sub>2</sub> = (1.0 atm)(2.0 L)/(0.50 L) = 4.0 atm.
cleanExplanation: At constant temperature, P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. The volume falls from 2.0 L to 0.50 L, a factor of 4 decrease, so the pressure rises by the same factor: P<sub>2</sub> = 1.0 atm × 2.0/0.50 = 4.0 atm.

work: Each Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> unit contains 3 sulfate groups × 4 O = 12 O atoms. n(O) = 0.50 mol × 12 = 6.0 mol.
cleanExplanation: In one formula unit of Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> there are three sulfate ions, giving 3 × 4 = 12 oxygen atoms. So 0.50 mol of the compound contains 0.50 × 12 = 6.0 mol of oxygen atoms.

work: n(H<sub>2</sub>) = 3.0/2.0 = 1.5 mol; n(O<sub>2</sub>) = 32/32 = 1.0 mol. 1.0 mol O<sub>2</sub> needs 2.0 mol H<sub>2</sub>, so H<sub>2</sub> is limiting. Water = 1.5 mol × 18 g/mol = 27 g.
cleanExplanation: Moles: H<sub>2</sub> = 3.0/2.0 = 1.5 mol and O<sub>2</sub> = 32/32 = 1.0 mol. The equation needs 2 mol H<sub>2</sub> per 1 mol O<sub>2</sub>, so 1.0 mol O<sub>2</sub> would require 2.0 mol H<sub>2</sub>; only 1.5 mol is present, making H<sub>2</sub> the limiting reagent. Then 1.5 mol H<sub>2</sub> gives 1.5 mol H<sub>2</sub>O = 1.5 × 18 = 27 g.

work: K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0, so 2x = 12 and x = +6.
cleanExplanation: Assign K = +1 and O = -2. The neutral salt requires 2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0, giving 2x = 12, so each chromium is +6.

work: Reverse the second equation (CO<sub>2</sub> → CO + ½O<sub>2</sub>, +283 kJ) and add it to C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> (-394 kJ). Sum: C + ½O<sub>2</sub> → CO, ΔH = -394 + 283 = -111 kJ.
cleanExplanation: Use Hess's law. Keep C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> (ΔH = -394 kJ) and reverse CO + ½O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> to get CO<sub>2</sub> → CO + ½O<sub>2</sub> (ΔH = +283 kJ). Adding and cancelling CO<sub>2</sub> leaves C + ½O<sub>2</sub> → CO with ΔH = -394 + 283 = -111 kJ.

work: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heat acts as a product. Raising T shifts the equilibrium left, lowering K because K depends only on temperature.
cleanExplanation: For an exothermic reaction, heat is released as a product. Raising the temperature adds heat, shifting the equilibrium towards N<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>. Because the equilibrium position moves to the reactant side, the equilibrium constant K decreases.

work: 60 min / 20 min = 3 half-lives. Remaining fraction = (1/2)<sup>3</sup> = 1/8.
cleanExplanation: 60 min is three half-lives (3 × 20 min). Each half-life halves the amount remaining, so the fraction left is (1/2)<sup>3</sup> = 1/8.
NaOH and HCl react 1:1. Moles of HCl = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 2.50 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol, so 2.50 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol NaOH is needed. Volume = 2.50 × 10<sup>-3</sup> / 0.125 = 0.0200 L = 20.0 mL.

work: Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> gives 2 OH<sup>-</sup> per unit, so [OH<sup>-</sup>] = 2.0 × 10<sup>-3</sup> M. pOH = 2.70, pH = 14.00 - 2.70 = 11.30.
cleanExplanation: Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> is a strong base that releases two hydroxide ions, so [OH<sup>-</sup>] = 2 × 0.0010 = 0.0020 M. pOH = -log(0.0020) = 2.70, and pH = 14.00 - 2.70 = 11.30.

work: R<sub>f</sub> = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front = 3.0 cm / 6.0 cm = 0.50. R<sub>f</sub> is always between 0 and 1.
cleanExplanation: The retention factor is the spot distance divided by the solvent-front distance: R<sub>f</sub> = 3.0/6.0 = 0.50. Values above 1 are impossible since a spot cannot travel beyond the solvent front.

work: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pK<sub>a</sub> + log([A<sup>-</sup>]/[HA]) = 4.76 + log(0.20/0.10) = 4.76 + 0.30 = 5.06.
cleanExplanation: Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH = pK<sub>a</sub> + log([CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>]/[CH<sub>3</sub>COOH]). The ratio is 0.20/0.10 = 2, and log 2 = 0.30, so pH = 4.76 + 0.30 = 5.06.

work: CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> (acetone) has a carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbon atoms, which defines a ketone.
cleanExplanation: The structure is CH<sub>3</sub>-CO-CH<sub>3</sub>: a carbonyl group whose carbon is bonded to two other carbons. That is the defining feature of a ketone (an aldehyde would have at least one H on the carbonyl carbon).

work: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> is an alkane (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>) with three chain isomers: pentane, 2-methylbutane (isopentane) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane).
cleanExplanation: Only three constitutional isomers exist for C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>: pentane (straight chain), 2-methylbutane (one branch) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (two branches on one carbon). All other namings reduce to one of these.

work: Br<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=C double bond, converting it to a single bond with one Br on each carbon. No atoms are lost, so this is an addition reaction.
cleanExplanation: Ethene's carbon-carbon double bond opens up and one bromine atom bonds to each carbon, giving 1,2-dibromoethane. Because the two reactants combine into a single product with no atoms lost, the reaction is an addition.

work: A peptide bond is an amide linkage formed by condensation between the -COOH of one amino acid and the -NH<sub>2</sub> of another, with loss of H<sub>2</sub>O.
cleanExplanation: The carboxyl group (-COOH) of one amino acid reacts with the amino group (-NH<sub>2</sub>) of the next, forming an amide (-CO-NH-) linkage and releasing one water molecule. This condensation is what joins amino acids into a peptide chain.

work: Leading zeros (0.00) are not significant; the significant digits are 3, 0, 4 and the final 0 after the decimal = 4 significant figures.
cleanExplanation: In 0.003040 the leading zeros only locate the decimal point and are not significant. The significant digits are 3, 0, 4 and the trailing 0 after the decimal (a trailing zero after a decimal point is significant), giving 4 significant figures.
Add the four measurements: 10.2 + 10.4 + 10.1 + 10.3 = 41.0. Dividing by the count (4) gives the mean: 41.0/4 = 10.25.
